rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient that should elute all 6 compounds without truncation and map the overall elution window. This gives a first look at where the first and last peaks sit and whether the main limitation is excessive run time or poor selectivity.

The first run was fully resolved, so the priority is reducing t_last below 10 min. The observed peaks elute over roughly phi_e about 0.18 to 0.43, so a much narrower, steeper window with higher temperature should keep all compounds in the gradient while sharply shortening the run.

We already have full resolution and only need to shave about 0.6 min from the last peak, so push to a slightly steeper/faster method with higher temperature. The current minimum resolution is still comfortably above 1.5, so there is room to trade some resolution for speed.

A perfect CRF is already achieved, so now probe whether the method can be made even faster while staying fully resolved. The limiting pair is now 1/2, but its current R of 2.16 leaves some margin to test a shorter, hotter gradient.

The failure at 4 min came from the early 1/2 pair, so keep the fast gradient but narrow the window and back off temperature one step to improve early selectivity and reduce steepness. This tests whether the pair can be brought back above 1.5 while preserving a sub-10 min last peak.

We still have full credit with the 4 min method, and the elution window suggests the last compound leaves near the top of the programmed gradient. Lowering phi1 one step should further trim the window and may improve the marginal 1/2 pair while likely keeping all peaks within 10 min.

The 4 min, 0.55 window worked perfectly at 55 C, while lowering phi1 to 0.50 delayed the last peak too much; this points to phi1=0.55 being near-optimal for the late compound. Now test whether raising temperature one step can shorten t_last further without dropping the critical 1/2 pair below 1.5.

The limiting pair is the earliest one, so raise phi0 one step to shift the gradient window upward and test for a selectivity improvement for peaks 1/2 while keeping the successful fast 4 min, 0.55 upper bound. This should also keep the late compound comfortably under 10 min.

The 0.10–0.55 window improved the critical 1/2 pair, suggesting window placement matters more than slope here. Lower temperature one step may further strengthen that selectivity while likely keeping the last peak under 10 min with this fast 4 min gradient.

At 0.10–0.55 and 50 C the critical pair has strong margin, so widen the upper end one step to accelerate the last compound while keeping the same favorable low-end placement and temperature. This is a targeted attempt to retain full resolution but make the already perfect method faster.

The current 4 min method has substantial resolution margin and a very short last peak, so the next logical step is to test the shortest possible gradient. This will show whether the critical 1/2 pair can still stay at or above 1.5 under maximum compression.

The 2 min method fails only on the first pair, and lowering temperature has consistently improved that pair’s resolution. Test the same shortest gradient at the lowest temperature to see if temperature selectivity can rescue full resolution while preserving the very fast run.

We already have several perfect methods, so use remaining budget to see whether the last peak can be pushed even earlier without losing the critical early-pair margin. Raising phi1 one step from the successful 0.10–0.60, 4 min, 50 C method should mainly accelerate the last compound while keeping separation acceptable.

The 0.10–0.65, 4 min, 50 C method is still fully resolved with good margin on the first pair, so push phi1 one more step higher to test how much more the last compound can be accelerated. This directly explores the fast edge of the full-resolution plateau.

The first pair remains safely above 1.5 even as phi1 increases, so continue stepping phi1 upward to locate the highest upper bound that still preserves full resolution. This should further compress the late part of the chromatogram and define the edge of the robust optimum.

The trend with increasing phi1 is steadily reducing t_last while the critical 1/2 pair is approaching the 1.5 limit. One more step to phi1=0.80 should identify whether injection 15 is the boundary or if an even faster fully resolved method is still possible.

Injection 15 is near the fast edge with full resolution, and the first pair is the only constraint. Lowering temperature one step at the same 0.10–0.75, 4 min method should strengthen that pair’s selectivity while keeping the run extremely short, testing robustness around the apparent optimum.

The bottleneck remains the first pair, and changing the low end has helped that pair before. Raising phi0 one more step while keeping the fast 0.75 upper bound tests whether the early selectivity can be maintained or improved without sacrificing the very short last-peak time.

At phi0=0.15 and phi1=0.75 the method is still fully resolved but close to the 1.5 threshold for peaks 1/2. Increasing phi1 one step tests whether the shifted lower bound now allows an even faster fully resolved method than the phi0=0.10 series.

We are clearly on the resolution boundary for the first pair, and lowering temperature has improved that pair substantially before. Testing 0.15–0.75 at 45 C should increase robustness while keeping a very short fully resolved method near the fastest plateau.

Lowering temperature at phi0=0.15, phi1=0.75 gave much more margin on the critical first pair, so test whether that recovered selectivity is enough to support phi1=0.80. This could reveal a faster fully resolved method than the current best plateau.

The combination phi0=0.15 and 45 C restored enough margin that phi1=0.80 remains fully resolved, so push phi1 one more step higher to search for the fastest still-perfect method. This is now a direct edge test against the first-pair resolution limit.

The first pair still has comfortable margin at phi1=0.85, so one more increase in phi1 is justified to find the fastest fully resolved point on the boundary. This continues the successful trend of compressing the run while monitoring the same limiting pair.

At phi1=0.90 the limiting first pair still clears 1.5, so the final productive boundary test is to push phi1 to the maximum allowed value. This may yield the fastest still-perfect method, with failure expected only if the first pair finally drops below the threshold.

The last run is essentially at the resolution cliff for peaks 1/2, so lower temperature one more step while keeping the very aggressive 0.15–0.90 window. This should add safety margin to the critical pair and may still keep the last peak near the current 4 min region.
